The Hadean Eon. This period spans Earth's first five hundred million years, from four point six to four point one billion years ago. It's named for Hades, the underworld, because of its hellish, molten conditions. The planet was still coalescing from cosmic dust, with a magma ocean covering its surface and no solid crust to speak of. Life had not begun, and the atmosphere consisted of unbreathable hydrogen and helium.

The Late Heavy Bombardment made up the final two hundred million years of the Hadean, bringing asteroids and comets that may have delivered water and organic molecules to Earth. Earth's Moon formed during this eon, likely from a giant impact with a Mars-sized body—a theory called the Giant Impact Hypothesis. The iron core separated and sank, releasing enough heat to keep the surface molten, and this planetary differentiation is still ongoing today.

No evidence of life survives from this eon—the temperatures and radiation made it utterly inhospitable. The Earth's magnetic field may have begun forming by the end of the eon as the liquid outer core started generating a dynamo. The Hadean left almost no rock record; any early crust was recycled or destroyed by the constant bombardment and geological upheaval.

This period precedes the Archean Eon, when the first stable crust crystallised, and both relate to the late heavy bombardment and the giant impact that created our Moon.
